subject: Activation steering transferability across model families as a function of representational similarity at intermediate layers

Topic: Activation steering transferability across model families as a function of representational similarity at intermediate layers

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-391)
response:
Activation steering works by adding a vector to a model's residual stream at inference time to shift its behavior — the central question here is whether a steering vector extracted from one model (say, Llama-3 70B) can be transplanted into a different model family (say, Mistral or Gemma) and still produce coherent, targeted behavioral change, and whether that transferability is predicted by how geometrically similar the two models' intermediate representations are. The key concepts are: (1) steering vectors, typically extracted as difference-in-means between contrastive activation pairs; (2) representational similarity metrics like centered kernel alignment (CKA) or Procrustes distance applied at matched layer depths; (3) the distinction between layer-wise similarity and functional similarity — two layers can have high CKA yet encode features in incompatible basis orientations. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the alignment problem at the subspace level: even if two models share a broadly similar representational geometry, the specific directions encoding a concept like "refusal" or "sentiment" may be rotated, scaled, or spread across a different number of dimensions, so a transplanted vector may activate the right neighborhood but trigger unintended features that happen to be co-localized in the target model's geometry. The subtler concern is that transferability results are highly sensitive to which layer you inject at — a vector that transfers cleanly at layer 16 of a 32-layer model may fail catastrophically at the functionally equivalent fractional depth in a 40-layer model, meaning naive depth-normalization is insufficient and you need empirical functional anchoring (e.g., matching layers by information-theoretic criteria or probing accuracy on shared tasks).

NEXT: If you find high CKA between two models at a given layer but the steering vector still fails to transfer, what are the two most mechanistically distinct explanations for that failure, and how would you design experiments to distinguish between them?

The first explanation is basis misalignment within a similar subspace: CKA is invariant to orthogonal transformations, so two models can score high CKA while the specific direction encoding, say, "hostile tone" points in completely different orientations in each model's residual stream — the subspace is shared but the basis is rotated, so injecting a vector that means "hostile" in model A injects noise or activates an unrelated feature in model B. The second is downstream circuit incompatibility: even if the injected vector lands correctly and activates the right feature representation at layer L, the MLP and attention circuits in subsequent layers of the target model may not "read" that feature the same way — Anthropic's dictionary learning work on Claude and Marks et al.'s circuit-tracing work both show that features are only meaningful relative to the downstream weights that process them, so a correctly placed vector can be functionally inert or misdirected if the consumer circuits differ. To distinguish these, you'd first apply a learned linear map (Procrustes-aligned or trained with a small probe dataset) between the two models' activation spaces before injecting — if transferability recovers, the problem was basis misalignment; if it doesn't, the subspace was fine but the downstream circuits are incompatible. A sharper test for the second mechanism is to freeze injection at layer L but vary the target model's subsequent layers by using activation patching to replace the target model's later-layer activations with the source model's — if behavioral effect recovers, you've isolated the failure to post-injection processing. Concretely, Merullo et al. (2024) on steering vector geometry and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis work (Huh et al., 2024) give you quantitative handles: models trained on more data converge toward a shared representation, but convergence is faster for semantic content than for the fine-grained directional structure that steering exploits.

This is consistent with Marks & Tegmark (2023) finding that the truth direction is roughly linear and transferable, while Arditi et al. The most informative geometric measurement next is the intrinsic dimensionality of the concept's activation cluster in each model — specifically, compute the participation ratio or explained variance curve of the top principal components of refusal-eliciting activations across a diverse prompt set in both models; if sentiment needs 2-3 dimensions and refusal needs 15-20, that quantifies why a rigid rotation fails for the latter. You'd then measure subspace overlap (principal angles between the top-k PCA components of refusal activations in each model) to test whether the high-dimensional refusal subspaces are even approximately aligned — if the largest principal angle exceeds 45 degrees, no linear map will work and you need a nonlinear alignment or concept-specific fine-tuning. This framing reframes the transfer problem: Procrustes recovery rate is a proxy for concept dimensionality and fine-tuning sensitivity, not just geometric similarity.

Anthropic's work on the "refusal direction" in Claude and Zou et al.'s representation engineering (2023) both implicitly support this split: the concept of harmfulness is present in base models (you can probe for it), but the behavioral response is post-RLHF, meaning transfer of the geometric direction doesn't guarantee transfer of the functional effect. To test this without intermediate checkpoints, you'd exploit the fact that several model families release both base and instruct variants with identical architecture — Llama-3 8B base vs. instruct, Mistral 7B base vs. instruct — letting you treat the base model as a synthetic "pre-RLHF" proxy and measure whether steering vectors extracted from one base model transfer more successfully (higher behavioral effect, lower required injection magnitude) to another base model than instruct-to-instruct transfer does. The sharpest measurement is injection magnitude at behavioral threshold: find the scalar multiplier needed to produce a detectable refusal-like output change, then compare that threshold across base-to-base, instruct-to-instruct, and cross-type transfer — if base-to-base requires smaller multipliers for equivalent effect, that's evidence the representations are more aligned; if it requires larger multipliers, the base model lacks the consumer circuits and the vector is geometrically landing but functionally inert. A confound to control for is that base and instruct models of the same family share pretraining weights, so any base-to-base similarity may reflect shared initialization rather than genuinely more universal representations — you'd need cross-family base comparisons (Llama base → Mistral base) to isolate the claim.

This would be strong evidence for what you might call circuit-representation dissociation: the geometry of the representation space is a necessary but not sufficient condition for behavioral outcomes, and RLHF is doing genuine circuit-level weight modification, not merely rotating the representation into a pre-existing behavioral slot — a conclusion with significant implications for whether steering is fundamentally limited as an alignment technique on base models. The failure mode to watch for carefully is partial effect: a base model under multi-layer injection might produce hesitation, topic-switching, or degraded fluency without clean refusal, which would suggest the consumer circuits are partially present from pretraining (plausibly from exposure to refusal-like text in web data) but not robustly wired — Geva et al.'s work on MLP layers as key-value memories suggests pretraining does install some behavioral tendencies that could act as weak consumer circuits. Jorgensen et al. (2023) on activation addition in GPT-2 and base Llama showed that multi-layer injection produces stronger and more coherent behavioral shifts than single-layer, but the effects were qualitatively different from RLHF'd behavior — more like thematic drift than structured refusal — which is exactly what circuit-representation dissociation predicts. If the intervention succeeds, that's equally informative: it would mean RLHF's primary contribution is representational amplification rather than novel circuit installation, which would suggest that sufficiently strong steering could substitute for alignment fine-tuning — a result that would be both practically important and somewhat alarming.

Conversely, if the residual difference is diffuse across output tokens and concentrated in late MLP layers, that suggests RLHF is primarily modifying the value-writing weights that translate features into output directions — closer to what Meng et al.'s ROME and MEMIT (2022-23) showed about factual recall being stored in mid-to-late MLP weights — and steering fails because it's injecting into the residual stream upstream of where the critical weight modifications live. The most alarming finding would be if the residual difference concentrates in attention head output weights (W_O) at specific heads known to implement induction or copying circuits — because that would mean RLHF is co-opting general-purpose computational machinery for refusal, wiring refusal into the basic information-routing fabric of the model rather than adding a separable module, which would explain why activation steering produces brittle or context-inconsistent refusal. Practically, this analysis frames a hard limit on steering as an alignment approach: steering can shift what information is present in the residual stream but cannot modify the operations performed on that information, so any behavior that requires new computational operations rather than amplified existing representations is fundamentally out of reach for inference-time intervention alone.

The "more room" intuition is plausible but probably wrong in its naive form: what matters isn't absolute depth but the ratio of pre-decision layers to post-decision layers, because the post-decision layers need sufficient capacity to consistently execute the refusal output given the early signal — a 96-layer model that makes its refusal decision at layer 20 has 76 layers of execution capacity, but if those layers are also doing heavy general reasoning, refusal execution can be overridden by downstream context integration, which is precisely the mechanism behind many jailbreaks that work by adding reasoning steps after the initial refusal signal. The cleaner hypothesis is that robustness scales with width-depth product at the decision layer, not depth alone — wider layers at the decision point mean more redundant circuits encoding the refusal feature, making it harder to ablate or steer away, which is consistent with Anthropic's finding that Claude 3 Opus is harder to jailbreak than Sonnet not just because it's deeper but because its attention heads at critical layers are wider and more redundant. Empirically isolating depth from parameter count is difficult because most scaling runs co-vary both, but the GPT-3 family and the Pythia suite (Biderman et al., 2023) offer some leverage: Pythia models at matched parameter counts but different depth/width aspect ratios show measurable differences in probe accuracy for safety-relevant concepts, with deeper-narrower models showing earlier crystallization of refusal-adjacent features in the logit lens but not necessarily more robust behavioral refusal under adversarial prompting. The most relevant empirical signal comes from activation patching studies on jailbreaks: Zheng et al. and related work show that successful jailbreaks tend to suppress the refusal signal at specific middle layers, and in larger models you need to suppress more layers simultaneously — which is indirect evidence for depth contributing redundancy, but the effect is confounded by the fact that larger models also had more RLHF compute and data. The sharpest honest answer is that current evidence doesn't cleanly separate depth from scale, and the field lacks a controlled experiment where identical RLHF procedures are applied to architecturally varied models (same params, different depth/width ratios) and refusal robustness is measured under standardized adversarial attack — that experiment is doable with the Pythia suite but hasn't been published to my knowledge.

The distributed-circuit hypothesis is compelling and has a concrete analogue in adversarial robustness literature for vision models, where certified robustness correlates with feature redundancy across layers rather than peak representational capacity at any single layer — the intuition translates directly: a refusal circuit that re-establishes its signal at layers 12, 24, and 36 independently is robust to suppression at any single intervention point, whereas a circuit that crystallizes once at layer 18 and merely propagates forward is vulnerable to a single targeted patch. Whether this emerges from scale or can be engineered is a real open question, but there's suggestive evidence it's partly implicit: Wei et al.'s jailbreak scaling results and Perez et al.'s work on prompt injection both show that larger models are harder to jailbreak with single-vector interventions but roughly equally vulnerable to multi-step attacks, which is exactly what you'd predict if scale produces distributed but not fully redundant circuits — you need more simultaneous suppressions, but the circuit still has exploitable chokepoints. Intentional engineering of distribution is theoretically possible through layerwise RLHF targeting: instead of standard DPO/PPO which applies gradient updates globally, you could compute refusal-probe accuracy at each layer during training and apply auxiliary losses that penalize low probe accuracy at early and middle layers simultaneously, forcing the model to develop early-layer refusal representations rather than delegating entirely to late layers. The practical obstacle is that this requires differentiating through the probe at each layer during RLHF, which is computationally expensive and may produce degenerate solutions where the model learns to activate the probe without the probe predicting actual behavioral refusal — a Goodhart problem at the representational level. The most honest framing is that current RLHF implicitly produces some distribution as a side effect of training on diverse refusal examples across context types, but it's uncontrolled and unevaluated — nobody has published a layerwise probe-accuracy curve across RLHF training steps showing whether distribution increases monotonically with training or plateaus early, and that curve would be one of the most useful empirical contributions the field could produce right now.
